money_at_stake.rationale: The global green methanol ships market, the commercial pool the Singapore bunkering buildout and the 112+ methanol-capable fleet sit inside, is valued at USD 7.57 billion in 2026, projected to grow to USD 46.25 billion by 2034 at a 25.39% CAGR. That places the leg in B1_10, near its upper end rather than crossing into B10_100; the occurrence's own dated commercial commitments (Singapore's five-year 2026-2030 bunkering licenses, Maersk's 18-25-vessel methanol fleet) are a real but still early slice of a market this size.

source_excerpt: The market is projected to grow from USD 7.57 billion in 2026 to USD 46.25 billion by 2034.

public_reach.rationale: A genuinely split pool. On the bunkering-supply side, Singapore licensed three companies for five years (2026-2030): Golden Island Pte Ltd and Global Energy Trading Pte Ltd are both independent Singapore-based private fuel suppliers with no public listing found this run, and the third, PetroChina International (Singapore) Pte Ltd, is a subsidiary of PetroChina Company Limited, which is listed (SSE: 601857, SEHK: 0857) but more than 82% owned by state-controlled China National Petroleum Corporation, so it sits closer to the state-entity end of the reach spectrum than a clean listed pure-play even though it technically trades. On the demand/shipowner side, reach is meaningfully stronger: A.P. Moller-Maersk (Nasdaq Copenhagen: MAERSK A/B, 2025 revenue USD 53.9 billion) is deploying 18 large methanol-enabled vessels delivered 2024-2025 with a stated plan to reach 25 by 2027, a large share of the cited 112+-vessel global methanol-capable fleet, and is unambiguously a clean listed name directly committing capital to this exact fuel transition. Scored at 45, the 'split, large unlisted/state share' anchor: real listed exposure exists on the demand side, and the supply/licensing side that this card's own retail_gap centers on is mostly private or state-majority-owned.

capture_odds.rationale: A real but bounded moat. Singapore, the world's largest bunkering port, selected only 3 of 13 applicants for exclusive five-year methanol-supply licenses, which is a genuine barrier to entry and a qualification-gated position rather than an open commodity market; Golden Island has already completed Singapore's first licensed methanol bunkering stem, converting the license into an operating, revenue-generating position rather than a paper award. Held at 48 rather than higher because methanol itself, once supplied, prices as a fungible marine fuel whose input costs (natural gas or biomass feedstock) and demand (still 112 vessels against roughly 105,000 ships in the world merchant fleet) leave the supplier side exposed to commodity-style margin compression once more capacity is licensed elsewhere, and because none of the three Singapore licensees, nor Maersk as the demand-side name, disclosed a methanol-specific margin figure this run could verify.

timing_fit.rationale: Money is moving now on a schedule already fixed independent of the IMO vote: Singapore's licenses took effect 2026-01-01 (this appraisal's anchor) and run through 2030, squarely inside the 2-5 year window, and Golden Island has already executed the first licensed methanol bunkering delivery under the new regime, confirming operational, not merely contractual, activity. Maersk's fleet build-out (18 vessels delivered 2024-2025, targeting 25 by 2027) runs on the same near-term cadence. Held at 75 rather than higher because the framework this occurrence is contrasted against, the IMO Net-Zero Framework itself, remains genuinely unresolved (its adoption vote postponed once already, not reconvening until fall 2026), so the larger regulatory tailwind that could accelerate the whole category beyond today's fixed licenses and fleet orders is not yet confirmed.
